title: Listening in pairs: two minutes, no fixing
description: One person talks, the other only listens and plays it back. A small exercise borrowed from counsellors that makes ordinary conversations feel completely different.

body.heading: The rules of the pair
paragraphs: Sit with one other person and set a timer for two minutes. One of you talks — about your week, a decision, anything real — while the other does three things only: listens, nods, and when the timer ends, plays back what they heard in their own words: 'So the hard part wasn't the work, it was not knowing where you stood.'

No advice. No fixing. No 'that reminds me of my…' — the listener's own stories stay parked until the swap. Then swap roles and repeat, so both people get a turn at the strange luxury of being fully heard.

body.heading: Why playback changes everything
paragraphs: Most of us listen while quietly rehearsing our reply, which means we hear the first half of everything and the second half of nothing. Playback removes the rehearsal: if you must say it back, you actually have to take it in.

Being played back accurately feels disproportionately good — it is proof, not politeness, that you were heard. And when the playback is wrong, the speaker can correct it, which fixes misunderstandings while they are still small and cheap.

body.heading: Use it beyond the exercise
paragraphs: You do not need a timer forever. Borrow the move inside real conversations: before responding to anything emotional, play back one sentence of what you heard. It slows arguments down, speeds understanding up, and works on teenagers, partners and parents alike.
Start with two minutes each, once. Most pairs are quietly astonished at how much fits into two minutes of being listened to properly.

takeaway: Two minutes of talking, no advice and no fixing — then play back what you heard, and swap. Being accurately heard is the whole gift.
